title: Phishing for Information: Spearphishing Service
summary: The parent technique describes phishing for information across any channel. This sub-technique narrows the channel to third-party services that the victim's employer does not control: personal webmail, social networks, chat platforms, and recruitment or freelance sites. The attacker creates or compromises an account there, then opens a conversation with a plausible business reason, such as a job offer or a supplier query. Because the message never passes the corporate mail gateway, content filtering, sender authentication checks, and attachment scanning do not apply to it. The only internal artefacts are the user's own browser or chat traffic to the service and whatever the user later types, forwards, or mentions. Detection therefore depends on endpoint and network visibility into consumer services plus user reporting, not on mail security controls.

beginner.definition: This sub-technique uses services outside your company, such as social media, personal webmail, or chat apps. The attacker makes a fake account or takes over a real one. Then they message an employee with a friendly reason to talk. It differs from the parent because the message never reaches your company mail system.
beginner.whyItMatters: Your company mail filters cannot check messages on someone else's platform. A fake recruiter on a social network can talk to your staff all day. The conversation looks normal, so the employee has no reason to suspect it. Information shared there, such as a project name or a tool you use, helps later attacks. Blocking every such site is rarely practical, so awareness matters more.
howItWorks: The attacker creates a profile or takes over an existing account on a public service.
They pick an employee whose public role makes the story sound believable.
They send a friendly message, for example a job offer or a supplier question.
They build trust over several friendly messages before asking for anything useful.
They ask small questions about your systems, your tools, and internal processes.
They record the answers and use them to plan a later attack.
beginner.example: Think of a shared office building where post for every company arrives at one front desk. Your own post room checks your letters. A stranger can still walk into the coffee shop next door. There they chat with your staff, and no post room sees the conversation. Messages sent through outside services are that coffee shop chat.
takeaways: Company mail filtering does not cover personal webmail or social messages.
Verify a recruiter or a supplier through a channel you already trust.
Small details add up to a useful picture, so remind staff about that.

objectives: Explain which services count as third-party communication channels.
Describe how an attacker builds a believable business pretext on those services.
Explain why corporate mail controls do not inspect this traffic.
Identify the endpoint and network artefacts that such conversations leave.
Describe how staff should verify an unexpected business contact.
